# Profile and validate columns {#sec-uc-profile}



Before a column is cleaned or matched on, it pays to know what is in it:
which formats occur, how often, and which values cannot possibly be right.
Two functions do most of that work. `string_shape()` reduces each value to
its *pattern* of character classes, and `valid_id()` checks the check digits
that most real-world identifiers carry. Together with `fcount()`,
`fparse_number()` and the strict date parsers they make a quick,
vectorised data-quality report.

| Question | Function |
|---|---|
| Which formats does this column hold? | `string_shape()` |
| Is this ABN / ACN / TFN / Medicare / card / ISBN / EAN / IBAN well formed? | `valid_id()` |
| How many digits, words or symbols per value? | `fcount()` |
| Do these amounts parse? | `fparse_number()` |
| Are these dates real calendar dates? | `fas.Date()` (`NA` for 31 June, 29 Feb 2023, ...) |

## What formats are in this column?

`string_shape()` replaces upper-case letters with `A`, lower-case letters
with `a` and digits with `9`, and keeps everything else. Tabulating the
shapes of a phone-number column shows its formats at a glance:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(3)
n <- 1e5
phone <- sprintf(
    sample(c("04%02d %03d %03d", "04%02d%03d%03d", "(07) %04d %04d",
             "+61 4%02d %03d %03d"), n, TRUE, prob = c(.5, .25, .15, .1)),
    sample.int(99, n, TRUE), sample.int(999, n, TRUE), sample.int(999, n, TRUE)
)
phone[sample(n, 40)] <- sample(c("unknown", "N/A", "0412 345 67",
                                 "call after 5pm", "1234"), 40, TRUE)

shape <- string_shape(phone)
sort(table(shape), decreasing = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
shape
   9999 999 999      9999999999  (99) 9999 9999 +99 999 999 999     9999 999 99         aaaaaaa  aaaa aaaaa 9aa             A/A            9999 
          49944           25146           14763           10107              14               9               7               6               4 
```


:::
:::


Four legitimate formats account for almost every row; everything with a
small count deserves a look. The ten-digit mobile number that lost a digit
(`9999 999 99`) is the kind of error no type check would catch:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rare <- names(which(table(shape) < 50))
unique(phone[shape %in% rare])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "unknown"        "0412 345 67"    "N/A"            "call after 5pm" "1234"          
```


:::
:::


`collapse = TRUE` reduces each run of one class to a single character,
which groups values by structure rather than length -- useful for free-text
or name columns, where exact lengths vary:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
string_shape(c("Smith", "SMITH", "O'Brien", "van der Berg", "J. Smith",
               "SMITH JNR", "Smith2"), collapse = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Aa"     "A"      "A'Aa"   "a a Aa" "A. Aa"  "A A"    "Aa9"   
```


:::
:::


Postcodes show how much a shape reveals with no domain rules at all -- the
letter O typed for a zero, a lost leading zero, a stray state or trailing
space:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pc <- c("4000", "0800", "800", "4OOO", "2000 ", "NSW 2000", "40000", NA)
data.frame(pc, shape = string_shape(pc))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
        pc    shape
1     4000     9999
2     0800     9999
3      800      999
4     4OOO     9AAA
5    2000     9999 
6 NSW 2000 AAA 9999
7    40000    99999
8     <NA>     <NA>
```


:::
:::


Letters and digits are classified by their Unicode category, so accented
and non-Latin letters count as letters and combining accents disappear into
the letter they modify.

## Validate identifiers

Most identifiers that people key in carry a check digit, chosen so that the
common typing errors -- one wrong digit, two adjacent digits swapped --
produce an invalid number. `valid_id()` checks them for the identifiers
that come up most in Australian and international data, ignoring spaces
and hyphens:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
valid_id(c("51 824 753 556", "51 824 753 557", "5182475355"), "abn")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
valid_id(c("2123 45670 1", "2123 45671 1", "7123 45670 1"), "medicare")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
valid_id(c("123 456 782", "123 456 789", "12345678"), "tfn")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]  TRUE FALSE    NA
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
valid_id(c("4111 1111 1111 1111", "4111 1111 1111 1112"), "luhn")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]  TRUE FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
valid_id(c("978-0-306-40615-7", "0-8044-2957-X"), "isbn")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
valid_id("GB82 WEST 1234 5698 7654 32", "iban")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::
:::


An 8-digit TFN gives `NA`: the older numbers use different weights, which
the ATO does not publish, so the function will not guess. Passing the check
does not prove that a number was ever issued -- only that it is not a
mistyped version of one.

To see how much this catches, take 5,000 well-formed ABNs, introduce a
one-digit typo into 150 of them and blank out 30:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(4)
cand <- sprintf("%011.0f", floor(runif(1e6, 1e10, 1e11)))
abn <- head(cand[valid_id(cand, "abn")], 5000)   # about 1 in 89 is valid
abn <- ifelse(runif(5000) < 0.5,
              sub("^(..)(...)(...)(...)$", "\\1 \\2 \\3 \\4", abn), abn)
typo <- sample(5000, 150)
substr(abn[typo], 5, 5) <- as.character(sample(0:9, 150, TRUE))
abn[sample(5000, 30)] <- NA

table(valid = valid_id(abn, "abn"), useNA = "ifany")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
valid
FALSE  TRUE  <NA> 
  131  4839    30 
```


:::
:::


Every invalid value is a typo, and every typo that changed a digit is
invalid: ABN's mod-89 check catches any single wrong digit. The typos it
"missed" put back the digit that was already there, or landed on a row that
was then blanked. Generating a million candidates and keeping the valid ones,
as above, is itself a vectorised call that takes a fraction of a second.

## A column profile

Put together, a few vectorised calls give a one-row summary per column that
is cheap enough to run on every column of every extract:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
profile_column <- function(x, id_type = NULL) {
    x <- as.character(x)
    shapes <- sort(table(string_shape(x, collapse = TRUE)), decreasing = TRUE)
    data.frame(
        n         = length(x),
        missing   = mean(is.na(x) | !nzchar(fsquish(x))),
        distinct  = length(unique(x)),
        shapes    = length(shapes),
        top_shape = names(shapes)[1],
        top_share = round(as.numeric(shapes[1]) / sum(!is.na(x)), 3),
        valid     = if (is.null(id_type)) NA
                    else round(mean(valid_id(x, id_type), na.rm = TRUE), 3)
    )
}
rbind(cbind(column = "phone", profile_column(phone)),
      cbind(column = "abn", profile_column(abn, "abn")))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  column      n missing distinct shapes top_shape top_share valid
1  phone 100000   0.000    98851      7     9 9 9     0.500    NA
2    abn   5000   0.006     4971      2   9 9 9 9     0.502 0.974
```


:::
:::


Extend it with whatever rules matter for the data: `fcount("[0-9]", x)`
for digits in name fields, `is.na(fparse_number(x))` for amounts that do
not parse, `is.na(fas.Date(x, "dmy"))` for impossible dates
(@sec-workflow shows the date parsers used this way).
